units: a woman coaching a group asks her students about aches that keep coming back
a boy describes a burning feeling in his thighs two days afterwards
that boy often gave up on the sessions at the end of the week
another student reports a comparable discomfort across her upper back
the coach puts these aches down to a sudden demand made on an unprepared muscle
she recommends a longer warm-up that begins with brisk walking
she advises closing the session with stretches free of any jerking
after a fortnight the aches ease and the absences stop growing
text: The coach asked her group about the aches that kept coming back after practice. One boy said his thighs burned two days later, and he owned up to dropping the sessions at the end of the week more often than not. A girl beside him reported the same discomfort, only across her upper back. None of that surprised the coach. Soreness turns up, she told them, when a muscle nobody has prepared is suddenly asked to give everything at once. So she stretched the opening of each practice, a good deal longer than before: brisk walking first, then slow circles of the arms and shoulders, then the drills themselves. She changed the closing minutes as well. Every session now finishes with quiet stretching, held steady and never yanked. A fortnight of that was enough. The aches eased off, and the empty spots along the wall stopped multiplying.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: contests of long ago were held with no measuring device and no markings on the ground
an elderly villager acted as judge through his word alone
the end of a match depended on the players wearing themselves out
in matches today the smallest irregularity is flagged and checked on video
athletes of long ago entered the game with no muscular preparation
that lack of preparation brought on repeated joint injuries
athletes today set aside a sizeable part of their training for warming up
the pull of movement and the wish to outdo the other person have not changed
text: Picture a match from long ago. No whistle, no clock, no lines painted on the ground. An old man from the village called it all, and whatever he said stood. The game ended when the players ran out of legs, and not a moment sooner. Now look at a match today. Shove somebody half a step too hard and it gets flagged, measured, and played back on a screen. The other gap is the getting ready. Back then you walked in cold and went straight at it, and you paid for that hurry with knees and ankles that wore out early. Players now hand over a solid slice of every training session just to wake the body up. One thing sits in both pictures, though. People run because running feels good, and because they want to beat whoever is next to them. The measuring changed. The wanting never did.

units: three signs give warning that an effort has outrun the resources on hand
the involuntary clenching of a muscle comes above all when water and minerals are short
a sharp pain under the ribs comes from breathing that has been handled badly
trembling in the legs shows an energy store that is close to empty
each of these signs calls for a different response
the first is answered by drinking and by lengthening the muscle gently
the second is answered by easing the pace and breathing more fully
the third is answered by stopping, taking in food and waiting
brushing these warnings aside opens the way to an injury that is slow to heal
text: Three signs warn an athlete that the effort has outrun the resources on hand. The first is the cramp: a muscle clamps down on its own and will not let go, and it turns up above all when water and minerals have run short. The second is a sharp jab under the ribs, and it comes from breathing that has been handled badly. The third is a tremor in the legs, which says the store of energy is close to empty. Each of the three calls for a different answer, and mixing them up only drags out the recovery. Against the first: drink, then lengthen the clenched muscle gently. Against the second: ease the pace and pull the breath deeper. Against the third: stop, take in food, and wait it out. Reading these warnings costs an athlete a pause. Brushing them aside opens the way to an injury that is slow to heal.

units: a smell of chalk and warm rubber fills the hall as the player walks in
this player had gone unused for the whole season
the person in charge of the team waves her onto the floor with a simple hand signal
her first plays go wrong and she misses two catches
a deflected ball strikes the edge of the hoop and drops back high in the air
she recovers the ball after its bounce by throwing herself to the ground
her roll ends with the ball sent back up by a single hand
the play earns her one point without changing the gap on the score
from that moment she stops staring at the ground and feels lighter
text: Chalk and warm rubber, that was the smell of the hall when the substitute finally set foot on the floor. She had gone the whole season unused, counting other people's passes. At the restart the man running the team waved her on with a flick of the hand, no words at all. Her first plays went wrong. She missed two catches and felt the quiet draw tight around her. Then a deflected ball clipped the edge of the hoop and dropped back high in the air. She followed the bounce, threw herself to the ground, rolled across one shoulder and sent the ball back up with a single open hand. The point counted. The gap on the scoreboard stayed exactly where it had been. Something else shifted, though: she stopped staring at the ground. The rest of the game felt short, and oddly light, as if the floor had agreed at last to hold her.

units: the item has to be pulled onto a limb that is straight and not bent
an item fitted over a folded joint slips away within the first few strides
the sleeve is drawn up from the lower leg and never rolled
a fold of fabric hampers the circulation and leaves the end of the limb numb
the central opening has to ring the kneecap without pressing on it
weight resting straight on the bone brings on a spread-out ache after the workout
the straps are tightened working from the bottom towards the top
tightening done the other way round makes the lower joint of the leg swell
wearing it at length for no reason weakens the muscles it covers
text: Pull the brace onto a straight leg, never onto a bent one. A support fitted over a folded joint slips away within the first few strides and stops holding anything at all. Draw the sleeve up from the lower leg, and never roll it, because a fold of fabric squeezes the vessels underneath and leaves the whole foot numb. Check next that the central opening rings the kneecap without pressing anywhere on it. Weight resting straight on the bone brings on a spread-out ache once the workout is over, and that ache can last the evening. Tighten the straps working from the bottom towards the top. Done the other way round, the pull drives blood downward and the lower joint of the leg swells. Take the brace off once the session ends. Worn at length for no reason, it weakens the very muscles it covers.

units: the management of a sports facility closes two halls for the time being
the buckled coverings of the floor had caused accidents
the relatives of the enrolled children protested against this decision
the facilities nearby had no free slot at all
a meeting open to the public was arranged
specialists pointed to an old water leak as the source of the trouble
that leak made the floorboards lift under the impact of jumps
the sports played with a racket or over a net move to a gymnasium brought back into service
the dance and strength sessions are held in a multipurpose hall
text: The management of the sports facility has closed two of its halls for the time being. The coverings on the floor there had buckled, and several people had come down hard on them. Relatives of the enrolled children protested at once, since the youngsters lost their slots and every facility nearby was already full. So a meeting open to the public was arranged. Specialists laid out what they had traced: an old water leak, never fully dealt with, which lifts the floorboards each time a jump lands on them. The answer comes in two parts. Everything played with a racket or over a net moves across to a gymnasium brought back into service. The dance and strength sessions go into a multipurpose hall. Repairs to the floors should be finished before the cold months, and the lost slots handed back.

units: two kinds of floor are fitted in most sports halls
these two floors answer differently under the weight of the foot
the boarding mounted on flexible supports sinks slightly with every step
this boarding hands part of the energy back to the leg
it spares the joints and forgives landings that come down badly
its pale shade holds the marks of shoes and calls for regular upkeep
the artificial floor grips more and helps the push at the start
it puts up with water, with wheels rolling over it and with shoes worn outdoors
it makes slides painful and takes none of the shock out of impacts
text: Most sports halls are floored in one of two ways, and the two do not answer the weight of the foot in the same manner. Boarding laid over flexible supports sinks a little under every step, then hands part of that energy back to the leg that produced it. It spares the joints, and it forgives a landing that comes down badly. Its pale shade, on the other hand, holds every mark a shoe leaves behind, so the upkeep has to be regular and thorough. The artificial floor grips harder and gives a cleaner push at the start of a sprint. Water does it no harm, wheels roll across it without leaving a trace, and shoes worn outdoors are welcome on it. What it will not do is soften anything: a slide across it hurts, and the shock of each landing travels straight up the leg with nothing taken out of it.

units: the writer holds that the mania for counting spoils the pleasure of physical activity
he sets out the effects of that mania one after another
he likens running to a graded test because of the devices worn on the arm
he notes that the setting of people against each other reaches even friendships
an easy outing turns in this way into a contest of figures
whoever falls short of the weekly target feels at fault despite having been active
night-time rest is submitted in its turn to the reading of graphs
the writer does not reject the indicators but blames them for filling the whole space
he wishes physical activity to remain a desire and not an obligation
text: Honestly, the mania for counting has eaten a good part of the pleasure out of moving. Look at what it has brought, one piece at a time. Running turned into a graded test: you set out with a device strapped to your arm and come home with a mark. Then the setting of one against another crept in everywhere, friendships included, so an easy outing turns into a contest of figures. After that comes the guilt. Whoever falls short of the weekly target feels at fault, though he walked, swam, and laughed with the people close to him. Even the sleep of the night goes into the graphs now, as if resting were something you could pass or fail. I am not saying the readings are worthless. I am saying they have filled the whole space between us. Moving ought to stay a desire, and never a debt you owe.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: this caregiver began her working life in a small local facility
there she eased the shoulders of swimmers during their training
she specialised in shoulder complaints, a specialty little sought after at the time
a women's squad at a high level then took her on
she watched the throwing movements through a whole season before stepping in
her way of going about it rested on video, on comparison and on talking
shoulder complaints fell within the group
she now leads the medical staff of a training centre
she credits her results to listening to the injured athletes and to checking what they said
text: The therapist began her working life in a small local facility, easing the shoulders of swimmers between one length and the next. From there she went deeper into shoulder complaints, a specialty few people were chasing at the time. A women's squad at a high level took her on, and she spent a whole season watching how the players threw before she stepped in with a single exercise. Her way of going about it caught everyone off guard. She filmed, she compared, she talked things over with the athletes rather than handing down orders. Shoulder complaints fell within the group. She now leads the medical staff of a training centre and teaches younger therapists. She says she invented nothing: she listened to the athletes who were hurting, then checked what they said, one claim at a time.

units: the performance leaves the viewer with an unsettling feeling
the performers were trained as athletes and not as stage artists
that background gives them an uncommon physical staying power
they dance for sixty minutes without their breathing showing any fatigue
that reserve lends an unexpected scale to the closing part
the same background produces the failing of the evening
trained to reach a goal, they favour movements that make a display
the gestures made for nothing, proving nothing, are what they lack
the string of feats leaves no room for a pause
the audience comes out impressed but barely moved
text: The performance leaves you unsettled, and the reason stands there from the opening minute: the performers were trained as athletes, not as stage artists. That background gives the evening its finest quality, a staying power you rarely see. They dance a full hour without their breathing showing any fatigue, and that reserve lends the closing part a scale no technique on its own would reach. The same background produces the failing of the evening. Trained to reach a goal, they go for the movement that makes a display: the high leap, the controlled fall, the shape that pulls a gasp out of the room. Gestures made for nothing, proving nothing, are what they lack. So the piece becomes one feat after another with nowhere to draw breath. You come out impressed, and barely moved by what you have watched.
